analysis.one_liner: Lets West Virginia permit coal trucks up to 126,000 pounds on a stretch of Interstate 77.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee in January 2007 and no vote was ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law generally caps truck weights on interstate highways at 80,000 pounds. This bill would carve out an exception for one 12-mile stretch of Interstate 77 in Kanawha County, West Virginia, letting the state issue special permits for coal-hauling trucks weighing up to 126,000 pounds. It was referred to committee, sent to a subcommittee, and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal producers and coal-hauling truckers on that route, who could move roughly half again more coal per trip, cutting their transport costs.

how_it_helps.text: Amends federal highway law to authorize West Virginia to issue special permits for vehicles up to 126,000 pounds gross vehicle weight hauling coal and coal by-products on Interstate 77 between Exits 85 and 97 in Kanawha County [S2][S3].

The exemption would let each truck carry substantially more than the standard 80,000-pound interstate limit, meaning fewer trips and lower per-ton hauling costs for coal moving on that corridor [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Other drivers on that stretch of I-77, who would share the road with much heavier trucks, and the public generally, which bears accelerated road and bridge wear and the safety risk of overloaded trucks.

drawbacks.text: Federal weight limits on interstates exist because heavier trucks impose more pavement and bridge damage and raise crash severity; a 126,000-pound exemption on a public interstate shifts those costs onto other road users and taxpayers [S2].

The bill applies to a single corridor for a single commodity, a narrow carve-out that invites similar exemptions for other states and industries rather than a general weighing of truck size and safety [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain is concentrated and modest: lower hauling costs for coal interests on one short corridor. The costs — faster road wear, heavier trucks mixed with ordinary traffic — are spread across drivers and taxpayers, and federal weight limits were set precisely to prevent that. As written, the benefits to the public are thin while the risks and costs are real, and the committee never tested the trade-off with a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its highways subcommittee, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Shelley Moore Capito introduced the bill on January 11, 2007 [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, where it remained [S5].
No hearings, markups, floor action, or votes are recorded; the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Motorists and taxpayers on that corridor are better off, since the heavier-truck exemption never became law; coal haulers lost the chance at cheaper transport.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Motorists and taxpayers; the exemption died

for.name: Rep. Shelley Moore Capito
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create the coal-truck weight exemption for her district's stretch of I-77.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never acted on it; the bill saw no markup, hearing, or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no cosponsors and never reached a vote, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition is recorded [S4][S5].

industries.note: Heavier permitted loads would cut their per-ton transport costs on a specific corridor, while the extra road wear and safety risk fall on other drivers and the public.

industries.industry: State and federal highway budgets / road users
industries.note: Trucks at 126,000 pounds impose pavement and bridge damage well beyond the standard limit; those maintenance costs are borne by the public highway system.
